hero.intro: There are two ways to build an online income. You can be a remote employee inside someone else's company, or you can be an independent contractor: a business of one who chooses the work, sets the price, and owns the relationship. DevUp is built for the second road. It is harder at the start and better at the top, and the one decision that shapes it most is who your clients belong to, an agency or you.
hero.creed: An employee is given clients. A contractor earns them. The earning is the harder path, and the only one where the upside is yours to keep.

mindset.title: You are not looking for a boss. You are looking for customers.
mindset.lead: This is the reframe that changes how you apply, price, and behave. An employee tries to be chosen and kept. A contractor tries to deliver an outcome and be rehired. Same person, completely different posture, and clients can feel which one you are in the first message.

rows.employee: The company hands it to you.
rows.contractor: You source it, and that skill never leaves you.
You do, per outcome, and you can raise it.

rows.employee: The company keeps the margin on your work.
rows.contractor: You keep it, and grow it as you specialize.

rows.employee: The company absorbs the dry spells.
rows.contractor: You do, so you build a runway and a pipeline.

rows.employee: Your time, forty hours at a stretch.
rows.contractor: A result. Once you sell results, hours stop being the ceiling.

mindset.note: The demand for this is not a fad. 77% of business leaders told Upwork they need fractional or independent talent. Companies increasingly want a specific skill for a specific window, not another full-time hire. That is a market built for a business of one.

roads.title: Agency or direct? Both are valid. Know what each one costs.
roads.lead: An agency places you with clients and takes a cut. Direct means the client is yours, with no one in between. Plenty of professionals start with an agency for the pipeline, then move to direct once they can sell for themselves. What matters is choosing with your eyes open, not by accident.

agency.title: Working through an agency
agency.blurb: A staffing firm or agency finds the client, handles the sale, and places you. You do the work; they manage the relationship and take a margin.
pros: A pipeline without the selling. The agency finds and closes clients, so you can start earning while you are still learning to sell yourself.
They handle the hard parts. Contracts, invoicing, collections, and disputes are their job, not yours.
A softer landing for beginners: structure, onboarding, and sometimes the mentorship a solo freelancer has to build alone.
Steadier income. A good agency keeps you booked, which smooths the feast-or-famine that direct work can bring early on.
A buffer against bad clients. If one pays late, the agency usually still pays you on schedule.
cons: They take a margin. The client pays more than you receive, and that gap is the agency's cut. It can be large.
You rarely own the relationship. Leave, and the client almost always stays with the agency. You cannot take them with you.
Less control over who you work with, the scope, and the rate. You mostly take what is assigned.
Possible exclusivity or non-compete terms that limit building your own direct clients on the side. Read the contract.
Your ceiling is their rate card. Raising your price means convincing the agency, not the client.

direct.title: Working with direct clients
direct.blurb: You find the client yourself and contract with them directly. No middleman, no margin taken, and no one else doing the parts an agency used to do for you.
pros: The whole rate is yours. No middleman margin, so the same client budget goes much further for you.
You own the relationship and the portfolio. Referrals, testimonials, and repeat work build into an asset nobody can revoke.
Full control: who you take on, the scope, the price, and how you work.
You can raise your rate directly with the client as you prove value, on your own timeline.
Every deal makes you better at sales, a skill that keeps paying for the rest of your career.
cons: You do your own selling. Finding and closing clients is now your job, and it never fully stops.
You run the business side: contracts, invoicing, chasing payments, and taxes.
Income can be lumpy, especially early. You carry the dry spells yourself, so you need a runway and a pipeline.
No safety net if a client pays late or disappears. Your contract and your systems are the only protection.
It is simply more to hold at once. The freedom and the responsibility are the same coin.

roads.verdict: A useful rule of thumb: an agency is a great way to start and to stay busy. Direct is where the rate and the ownership live. Many pros run both at once, an agency retainer for the floor and direct clients for the ceiling. Choose on purpose, and revisit the choice as your ability to sell for yourself grows.

getDirect.title: Direct clients don't fall from the sky. They are built, step by step.
getDirect.lead: This is the part that scares people off direct work, and it is a learnable process, not a personality trait. You do not need to be an extrovert or a salesperson. You need a clear position, real proof, and a repeatable way to start conversations. Here is the sequence.

steps.title: Get specific about who you help
steps.how: Pick a narrow lane and a clear outcome. I keep Shopify stores' books clean, not I do admin. Specific is easier to refer, easier to trust, and easier to price.

crossref.label: Pick your lane with the rubric

steps.title: Build proof before you pitch
steps.how: Ship two or three real, visible pieces of work, even self-made or for a cause you like. Nobody hires a claim. They hire evidence they can see.

steps.title: Turn your warm network on first
steps.how: Tell everyone you know, former colleagues, batchmates, past clients, exactly what you now do and who you help. Your first direct clients almost always come from people who already trust you.

steps.title: Do focused outbound
steps.how: Make a short list of businesses that fit your lane and reach out with one specific, useful observation about their work, not a generic I am available. A good list beats a big one.

steps.title: Let content pull people in
steps.how: Post what you know where your clients look, a tip, a teardown, a before-and-after. Over time it makes clients come to you, already half-sold. Slow to start, compounding forever.

steps.title: Run the discovery call like a diagnosis
steps.how: Ask more than you pitch. Understand the client's real problem and what a good outcome is worth to them before you ever talk price. You are prescribing, not selling.

steps.title: Propose the outcome, not the hours
steps.how: Send a short proposal that restates their goal, your plan, the deliverables, and a clear price. Sell the result you will produce, not the time you will spend.

crossref.label: Write it from a blank page

steps.title: Convert one-off wins into retainers
steps.how: After you deliver, propose the ongoing version, the monthly relationship that turns a project into predictable income. Retainers are how direct work becomes stable.

getDirect.note: None of this needs cold charm or a big following. It needs a specific promise, evidence you can point to, and the discipline to keep the pipeline full before you need it. DevUp has a workshop for each piece. The links take you there.

protect.title: No agency is standing behind you now. Your contract is.
protect.lead: The freedom of direct work comes with the responsibility an employer used to carry. In the Philippines there is still no dedicated law that will collect an unpaid invoice from a foreign client for you, which is exactly why the habits below are not optional paperwork. They are the only protection that actually holds.

items.title: There is still no freelancer protection law
items.desc: The Freelance Workers Protection Act, written contracts, upfront payment, penalties for non-payment, passed the House in 2023 and then stalled. It is not yet law. So you cannot lean on a statute. You have to build the protection into every deal yourself.

source.label: BusinessMirror, Bill seeks protection for freelancers, gig workers

items.title: Contract, scope, and a deposit, every time
items.desc: Written scope so done is defined, milestones so you are never carrying weeks of unpaid work, and a deposit before you start. Build the habit now while the stakes are small, so it is automatic when they are large.

items.title: Register, and invoice like a supplier
items.desc: A registered freelancer in the Philippines can use the 8% flat-tax option (on gross receipts above ₱250,000, if you stay under the ₱3M VAT threshold) and issue a proper invoice. These figures are current as of Taxumo's 2025 guide; BIR thresholds can change, so reconfirm them yearly before you file. Being invoice-ready is itself a rate differentiator, because it lets a serious client book you as a real supplier, not a favor.

source.label: Taxumo, Taxes for Freelancers in the Philippines (2025 guide)

items.title: Get paid through channels that protect you
items.desc: Use tracked, professional payment rails and keep the paper trail. Never move work off-platform to save the fee before trust is earned, and treat any unfunded milestone as unpaid work, because that is what it is.

closing.title: Own the relationship, and you own the career.
closing.body: An agency can hand you a client and take them back just as easily. A skill you can sell yourself, position, proof, a full pipeline, is an asset nobody can revoke. Start wherever gets you moving, agency or direct. But build the ability to win a client on your own, because that is the thing that makes you a business instead of a seat someone rents.
closing.point: Pick your next move. Each one is a workshop, not a lecture. You leave with something built.
